added_claims.speaker: Tom Roble
added_claims.quote: they are looking more and more to Alternative strategies to fill maybe the void left by bonds
added_claims.claim: US allocators building 'robust' portfolios increasingly use uncorrelated alternative strategies to fill the diversification gap left by bonds, driven by worry that equity returns will slow.
added_claims.direction: flows toward diversifiers, away from bonds
added_claims.conditions: while bonds fail to diversify equities

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: if you're a big allocator and you can compress people on fees you'll tend to structurally outperform as well
added_claims.claim: Large institutional CTA allocators structurally beat the index partly by negotiating lower fees than the headline fees embedded in index returns, the same fee edge replication exploits.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: that's before somebody else's fees on that maybe it's in other words there may be implementation fees that we don't see when you're looking at those numbers
added_claims.claim: Index return comparisons (e.g. the Bridge Alternatives managed-account index) may exclude implementation or platform fees and need minimums, so their returns overstate what an investor actually gets.

added_claims.speaker: Tom Roble
added_claims.quote: you're tracking an e an evolving portfolio you're not tracking a portfolio which is a static portfolio every year we change the constituents
added_claims.claim: Tom challenges the 'unchanging index' claim: a replicator's principal-component weights shift and it tracks an index whose constituents and their models change yearly, so its implementation evolves much like a CTA's research process.
added_claims.testable: partly - track replicator factor weights over time

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: absolutely not those guys are agreable there's sharp ratios of 2.2 or whatever um no look the thing about replication is you have to know what you can replicate
added_claims.claim: Multi-strategy pod shops with Sharpe ratios around 2 cannot be replicated, because replication works only where returns come from a few liquid factor exposures, as with trend CTAs.
added_claims.conditions: replicable only when returns load on liquid factors
added_claims.testable: yes - out-of-sample factor-replication R2 by strategy type

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: it's not that people can't see the benefits it's they feel it shouldn't work because past prices are not supposed to be indicative of future performance
added_claims.claim: Allocators under-allocate to trend following not because they miss the statistical benefits but because they believe past prices should not predict returns (efficient-market prior), so the strategy lacks a credible story for them.

added_claims.speaker: Tom Roble
added_claims.quote: the way the regory to is interpretated is there shouldn't be any exposure to Commodities
added_claims.claim: UCITS/ESMA rules are commonly read as banning direct commodity exposure, splitting European investors between dropping commodities from CTA products and adding them back through bank structured notes.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: you're not going to find out what they really think until you're standing in front of them
added_claims.claim: Stated investor demand (e.g. everyone wants a top CTA in an Article 9 wrapper) is unreliable; real demand shows only when a concrete investable product is offered.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: Andrew Beer says this, citing an SG investor survey by Tom ('Tom in his investor survey ... came out a couple of months ago'); Tom does not state it himself.
corrections.fix: Andrew Beer, citing Tom's SG investor survey: about a quarter of European investors want ESG-sensitive products and many cannot hold commodities, creating demand for non-commodity CTA exposure.

corrections.issue: Range misstated: Tom says AUM has bounced between $300bn and $350bn since 2014 (the $350-400bn range is Niels's Barclay Hedge recollection).
corrections.fix: Managed futures AUM grew to about $350bn in 2009-10 and, per Tom, has stayed between about $300bn and $350bn since 2014 (Niels recalls $350-400bn from Barclay Hedge), with the main increase after strong 2022 performance.

completeness_estimate: 0.87 - speaker attribution in the unlabelled captions is right except one claim (C21-2); first reader caught all main arguments but missed a few caveats (fee data, index evolution counterpoint, replicability limits, stated vs revealed demand).
